newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten calls China's plan for HK laws "repugnant".
newsitem.headline: Patten calls China's plan for HK laws "repugnant".

text.p: In his strongest worded attack yet, Governor Chris Patten lashed out on Thursday at China's proposal to dilute Hong Kong's civil liberties laws, including its bill of rights.
On the eve of a debate in Beijing on the proposals, Patten warned the "repugnant" proposals, if passed, would seriously damage Hong Kong.
"Nobody who has spent more than a few minutes in Hong Kong over the last few days can be in any doubt that they are repugnant to the community," Patten said in a statement.

China's handpicked Preparatory Committee of 150 Chinese and Hong Kong officials, responsible for transforming the British colony into a Special Administrative Region of China, begins a two-day meeting on Friday at which the proposal on the laws is high on the agenda.

Patten warned the proposals, if passed, would breach China's promise to accord Hong Kong the "high degree of autonomy" contained in the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration, the treaty governing the handover of the territory to China at midnight on June 30.

The treaty embodies Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's "one country, two systems" vision which promises Hong Kong people will run Hong Kong and will be permitted to maintain their freedoms and capitalist way of life intact for 50 years.
"On few issues over the years has there been such a clear and broad consensus, embracing almost all shades of the political spectrum," Patten said.

"To these voices have been added those overseas -- including not only British ministers but most recently President Clinton -- who wish Hong Kong well, and who want to believe in 'one country, two systems', but who are deeply concerned at the prospect Hong Kong's freedoms will be eroded.

"If, in the light of these opinions and the advice which it will no doubt hear from those of its members who have been appointed to speak for Hong Kong people, the Preparatory Committee decides to draw back from endorsing these ideas, Hong Kong will breath a sigh of relief, and the 'one country two systems' model will pass, and be seen to pass, one of the stiffest tests which it has so far faced.
"If not, the damage to Hong Kong will be enormous and irrevocable."

"Hong Kong is entitled to know, before 1 July, whether China still believes in 'one country, two systems' or whether it now wants to impose 'one country, one system' in contravention of its international obligations and its solemn promises to the six million people of Hong Kong."
